title: The Trial Before Pilate and Herod, the Cross, and the Burial
summary: The council brings Jesus to Pilate on political charges. Pilate finds no basis for them, sends Jesus to Herod Antipas, and three times declares him innocent, but under the crowd's pressure releases the insurrectionist Barabbas and hands Jesus over to be crucified. On the way Jesus warns the mourning women of Jerusalem; on the cross he prays for those who crucify him, promises paradise to a repentant criminal, and commits his spirit to the Father. A centurion calls him righteous, the crowds go home beating their breasts, and Joseph of Arimathea buries him in a new tomb while the women from Galilee watch.
story:
This chapter is the lowest point of Luke's story and, as chapter 24 will show, its turning point. Everything Jesus foretold on the road to Jerusalem now happens: he is handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, insulted, and killed (18:32-33). Simeon had said that the child would be a sign that would be opposed and that a sword would pierce his mother's soul (2:34-35), and Jesus had said he must be numbered with the transgressors (22:37). Now he hangs between two criminals.

Luke stresses again and again that Jesus is innocent. Pilate says so three times (verses 4, 14-15, 22), Herod finds nothing deserving death (verse 15), one of the criminals says ‘this man has done nothing wrong’ (verse 41), and the centurion calls him righteous (verse 47). Yet the innocent one dies alongside the guilty, and a man imprisoned for insurrection and murder goes free in his place (verse 25). Luke also shows mercy flowing from the cross: Jesus prays for forgiveness for those who crucify him (verse 34) and promises paradise to a dying criminal (verse 43). The crowds who watched go home grieving (verse 48), and the women who followed from Galilee see where he is buried (verse 55), which matters for the next chapter: they will know which tomb is empty. The chapter ends in silence, with the Sabbath beginning and the women resting according to the commandment.
historical:
Pontius Pilate governed Judea as prefect from about AD 26 to 36. A limestone block found at Caesarea Maritima in 1961 records his dedication of a building to Tiberius and gives his title as praefectus Iudaeae. Philo (Embassy to Gaius 299-305) and Josephus (Jewish War 2.169-177; Antiquities 18.55-62, 85-89) describe him as harsh and provocative, and Luke himself mentions Galileans whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices (13:1). Tacitus, around 116, records that Christus was executed under Tiberius by the procurator Pontius Pilate (Annals 15.44). The charges brought to him (verse 2) were chosen to matter to Rome: misleading the nation, forbidding the payment of tribute to Caesar (which 20:20-25 shows to be false), and claiming to be Messiah, a king.

Only Luke records the hearing before Herod Antipas (verses 6-12). Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea as tetrarch from 4 BC until AD 39, when the emperor Gaius deposed him and sent him into exile (Josephus, Antiquities 18.240-255). He had imprisoned and beheaded John the Baptist (3:19-20, 9:7-9; Antiquities 18.116-119), and Pharisees warned that he wanted to kill Jesus, whom Jesus called ‘that fox’ (13:31-32). Luke had sources near his court: Joanna, wife of Herod's steward Chuza (8:3, 24:10), and Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod (Acts 13:1). Pilate's move was a courtesy rather than a legal necessity; a governor normally tried a case where the offense was committed, and Felix later asks what province Paul is from before deciding to hear him himself (Acts 23:34-35). A. N. Sherwin-White's Roman Society and Roman Law in the New Testament (1963) set the trials of Jesus and Paul against this legal background. The enmity between Herod and Pilate (verse 12) is not explained; Pilate's killing of Galileans (13:1) may have played a part, and Philo reports that the sons of Herod the Great protested when Pilate set up gilded shields in Jerusalem (Embassy to Gaius 300). The historicity of the scene is debated. Martin Dibelius (‘Herodes und Pilatus’, 1915) argued that it grew out of Psalm 2:1-2, which Acts 4:25-27 applies to Herod and Pilate; Harold Hoehner (Herod Antipas, 1972) and others answer that Luke's sources, the plausibility of Antipas being in Jerusalem for the feast, and the scene's lack of any legal result argue for a real memory rather than an invention.

Crucifixion was the Roman punishment for slaves, violent criminals, and rebels, meant to be slow, public, and shameful. Cicero called it the cruelest and most disgusting penalty (Against Verres 2.5.165). In 1968 an ossuary found at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in Jerusalem held the heel bone of a man named Yehohanan with an iron nail still through it, the only skeletal evidence of crucifixion from Roman Judea, showing that victims were nailed and that a crucified man could be buried in a family tomb. The Law forbade leaving an executed man hanging overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22-23), and Josephus notes that Jews took down and buried even the crucified before sunset (Jewish War 4.317). The place called The Skull (Golgotha in Aramaic, Calvary from the Latin calvaria) lay outside the walls; the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, dedicated in 335, marks the traditional site, and excavations show the area was a disused quarry with rock-cut tombs. The darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour (verse 44) could not have been a solar eclipse, since Passover fell at full moon. The Christian chronographer Julius Africanus, in the early third century, made that point against a writer named Thallus who had explained the darkness as an eclipse (preserved by George Syncellus).
cultural:
Roman practice distinguished a beating given as a warning from the flogging that preceded crucifixion. Pilate twice offers to ‘punish’ Jesus and release him (verses 16 and 22), using paideuō, a word for discipline, which suggests the lesser beating. Herod's soldiers dress Jesus in a bright or splendid robe (esthēta lampran, verse 11), mocking his claim to kingship; Luke uses the same noun for the dazzling clothing of the angels at the tomb (24:4) and for the royal robe Herod Agrippa wore on the day of his death (Acts 12:21). Luke omits the Roman soldiers' crown of thorns and purple cloak that Mark and John describe; in his account the mockery at the trial comes from Herod's men.

Simon of Cyrene came from a Greek city in North Africa with a large Jewish community; Cyrenian Jews had a synagogue in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9). Roman soldiers could press a civilian into carrying a load. Luke adds that Simon carried the cross ‘behind Jesus’ (opisthen, verse 26), the posture of the disciple who takes up his cross and follows (9:23, 14:27). The women who mourn (verse 27) were doing what Jewish women did at funerals, beating the breast and wailing, and public lament for a condemned man carried risk. Jesus turns their grief toward the suffering coming on the city. His saying about the barren (verse 29) reverses the blessing spoken to his mother (1:42, 11:27), and his words about the mountains and hills quote Hosea 10:8, words Revelation 6:16 also uses. The proverb about green and dry wood (verse 31) argues from the lesser to the greater: if they do this when the tree is green, to the innocent, what will happen when it is dry?

The executioners' division of the clothing echoes Psalm 22:18, and the sneering rulers echo Psalm 22:7. The sour wine (oxos) the soldiers offer (verse 36) was the cheap, vinegary wine of soldiers and laborers, and Psalm 69:21 speaks of sour wine given to the sufferer. The hours are counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon and the ninth about three in the afternoon, the hour of the afternoon sacrifice and prayer in the temple (Acts 3:1). Jesus' last words, ‘Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit’ (verse 46), are Psalm 31:5 with ‘Father’ added, a psalm of trust that later Jewish prayer uses before sleep and that closes the hymn Adon Olam. Beating the breast was a sign of grief and contrition, as with the tax collector in the temple (18:13). Paradise (paradeisos) came into Greek from Persian, where it meant an enclosed park or garden, and the Septuagint uses it for the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:8). In Jewish writings of the period it could name the place where the righteous dead await the resurrection, and a saying attributed to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai in the Babylonian Talmud speaks of two roads before the dying, one to the Garden of Eden and one to Gehinnom (b. Berakhot 28b). Joseph's request for the body was bold for a council member, and Luke notes that the tomb had never been used (verse 53), as the colt of the entry had never been ridden (19:30). The Sabbath was ‘beginning’ (epephōsken, verse 54), literally ‘dawning’, perhaps from the lamps lit at sunset on Friday.
literary:
Luke tells the passion in a sequence of scenes: Pilate (verses 1-7), Herod (8-12), Pilate again (13-25), the road (26-32), the cross (33-43), the death (44-49), and the burial (50-56). Repetition carries his emphasis. Pilate's verdict of innocence comes three times, matching Peter's three denials in the previous chapter, and three groups mock Jesus at the cross, the rulers, the soldiers, and one criminal, with the same taunt: save yourself (verses 35, 37, 39). The irony is that he saves others precisely by not saving himself, and at that very moment he saves the second criminal. The word ‘today’ (sēmeron, verse 43) closes a thread that runs through the Gospel: today a Savior is born (2:11), today this Scripture is fulfilled (4:21), today salvation has come to this house (19:9).

Luke reshapes the scene he shares with Mark. He omits the cry ‘My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?’ and gives instead three sayings found only in his Gospel: the prayer for forgiveness (verse 34), the promise to the criminal (43), and the final prayer from Psalm 31:5 (46). He places the darkness and the tearing of the temple curtain together before Jesus' death (verses 44-45), where Mark and Matthew place the tearing after it, so that the two signs frame the last cry. And he has the centurion praise God and call Jesus ‘righteous’ (dikaios) rather than ‘Son of God’, the word that sums up Luke's case for Jesus' innocence and recalls the righteous sufferer of the Psalms and the righteous Servant of Isaiah 53:11.

The chapter is built to be read with Acts. Herod and Pilate, enemies made friends, are named together in the church's prayer (Acts 4:27). Paul, like Jesus, is tried before a Roman governor and a Herodian king, Agrippa II, who both find him innocent (Acts 25-26). Stephen dies with two prayers that echo verses 34 and 46: ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit’ and ‘Lord, do not hold this sin against them’ (Acts 7:59-60). Peter tells the people of Jerusalem that they and their rulers acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17), which matches ‘they do not know what they are doing’. The disciple's road is traced in the master's.

doctrines.note: Luke's story shows the exchange at the heart of the cross. Barabbas, imprisoned for insurrection and murder, is released, and Jesus, declared innocent three times, dies in his place (verse 25). The innocent one is numbered with the transgressors, as Jesus said Scripture required (22:37), and his first word from the cross is a prayer for the forgiveness of those who put him there (verse 34).

The criminal has no time to do anything but fear God, confess his guilt, recognize Jesus' innocence, and ask to be remembered in his kingdom (verses 40-42). Jesus promises him paradise that same day (verse 43). Salvation is received, not earned, and the dying man becomes the first person in Luke to be promised a place with the crucified Christ.

“Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise” (verse 43), with Jesus' committal of his spirit to the Father (verse 46), is a key text for the state of believers between death and resurrection. Most Christian traditions read it as a promise of conscious fellowship with Christ immediately after death, though they differ on where paradise is; others, placing the comma after ‘today’, read it differently (see the hard question).

The inscription names Jesus ‘the King of the Jews’ in mockery (verse 38), the soldiers taunt him as king (verse 37), and the criminal asks to be remembered when he comes into his kingdom (verse 42). Joseph of Arimathea was waiting for the kingdom of God (verse 51). Luke shows the kingdom arriving where no one expected it: in a crucified king who opens paradise to a condemned man.

The chapter is full of human decisions, the council's, Pilate's, Herod's, and the crowd's, and Luke holds each responsible. Yet the Gospel and Acts present these same events as what God had determined (22:22) and what his hand and plan had decided beforehand should happen (Acts 4:27-28). Human evil does not defeat God's purpose; it is made to serve it.

words.note: Paradeisos, paradise. It occurs only three times in the New Testament: here (verse 43), for the third heaven into which Paul was caught up (2 Corinthians 12:4), and for the place of the tree of life in the paradise of God (Revelation 2:7). Borrowed from a Persian word for an enclosed park, it is the Septuagint's word for the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:8) and for royal parks (Nehemiah 2:8), and in Jewish writings of the period it could name the dwelling of the righteous dead or the restored Eden of the age to come. Jesus promises the criminal Eden restored, and above all his own company: ‘with Me’.

Dikaios, righteous, just, innocent. It occurs about 79 times in the New Testament and 11 in Luke. Luke uses it for Zechariah and Elizabeth (1:6) and Simeon (2:25), and for Joseph of Arimathea in this chapter (verse 50). The centurion's words, “Surely this was a righteous man” (verse 47), sum up Luke's emphasis on Jesus' innocence, where Mark has ‘Son of God’. In Acts the apostles call Jesus ‘the Righteous One’ (Acts 3:14, 7:52, 22:14), a title that recalls the righteous Servant who justifies many (Isaiah 53:11).

Katapetasma, curtain or veil. It occurs six times in the New Testament: once in each Synoptic account of the passion and three times in Hebrews (6:19, 9:3, 10:20). In the Septuagint it can name both the screen at the entrance of the sanctuary and the inner curtain before the Most Holy Place, where only the high priest entered on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:2). Luke does not say which curtain tore, and Josephus describes both (Jewish War 5.212-214, 219). Hebrews reads the curtain as the way into God's presence now opened through Christ's flesh (10:19-20).

Aphiēmi, to let go, release, leave, and so to forgive, cancel a debt. It occurs about 146 times in the New Testament and 32 in Luke, where it covers both leaving (nets and homes, 5:11, 18:28) and forgiving (5:20-24, 7:47-49, 11:4, 17:3-4). In verse 34 Jesus asks the Father to forgive those who crucify him, doing what he taught in the Lord's Prayer (11:4) and in the Sermon on the Plain: love your enemies and pray for those who mistreat you (6:27-28). Stephen will pray the same way (Acts 7:60).

Sōzō, to save, rescue, heal, preserve. It occurs about 107 times in the New Testament and 17 in Luke, four of them in the mocking of this chapter (verses 35, 37, 39). Earlier in Luke it meant healing and rescue as well as salvation from sin: your faith has saved you (7:50, 8:48, 17:19, 18:42), and the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10). The rulers concede that he saved others, and all three taunts demand that he save himself. The irony is that his refusal to save himself is the way he saves.

Mimnēskomai, to remember, call to mind. It occurs 23 times in the New Testament, six in Luke. In Scripture, God's remembering is not recalling a forgotten fact but acting on a commitment: God remembers Noah (Genesis 8:1), his covenant (Luke 1:72), and his mercy (1:54). The criminal's plea, ‘Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom’ (verse 42), echoes the prayers of the Psalms (Psalm 106:4) and Joseph's request to the cupbearer, who forgot him (Genesis 40:14, 40:23). Jesus does not forget; he answers with today.

Paideuō, to train, discipline, correct, and in a legal context to punish by beating. It occurs 13 times in the New Testament, twice in this chapter, both times in Pilate's offer to ‘punish Him and release Him’ (verses 16, 22). Elsewhere it describes Moses' education (Acts 7:22), God's fatherly discipline of his children (Hebrews 12:6-10), and grace training believers (Titus 2:12). Pilate's word suggests a warning beating rather than the scourging before crucifixion, a compromise he offers twice and abandons.

christ:
The cross is the center of the Christian confession, and Luke shows who is dying on it. He is the King of the Jews, as the inscription says in mockery and as the reader knows in truth, the Son of David whose kingdom the angel promised would never end (1:32-33). He is ‘the Christ of God, the Chosen One’ (verse 35), titles the rulers use to sneer and that the voice from heaven used at the transfiguration (9:35). He is the righteous one of the Psalms, whose garments are divided (Psalm 22:18), who is mocked (Psalm 22:7), given sour wine (Psalm 69:21), and who dies entrusting his spirit to God (Psalm 31:5). He is Isaiah's Servant, counted among the transgressors, who bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12), and here he intercedes for them in so many words.

The three sayings in Luke's account show what kind of death this is. ‘Father, forgive them’ shows the Son praying for enemies to the end, the forgiveness he taught becoming the forgiveness he gives. ‘Today you will be with Me in Paradise’ shows the dying King exercising royal authority, opening Eden to a criminal while he himself is being executed as one. ‘Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit’ shows the Son's trust in the Father unbroken even in death; the Gospel that began with the boy in his Father's house (2:49) ends his earthly life with the Father's name on his lips. Luke gives no theory of the atonement in this chapter, but the exchange he narrates is unmistakable: the guilty Barabbas is released and the innocent Jesus dies; a criminal who deserves his sentence (verse 41) is promised paradise by the one who does not deserve his.

The church confesses that here, in a public and shameful Roman execution, the Son of God gave his life for sinners, and that this death is not the end of the story but the means by which God saves. The darkness and the torn curtain signal that something has happened between God and his people and between heaven and earth: judgment on a world that crucifies its Lord, and a way opened into God's presence. The Gospel will not let the reader look away from the burial, because the resurrection it proclaims is the resurrection of this crucified and buried body.
interpretation:
The church read this chapter through the Psalms from the start. The apostles' prayer in Acts 4:25-27 applies Psalm 2 to Herod and Pilate gathered against the Lord's anointed. The second-century Gospel of Peter goes further than Luke, making Herod the one who orders the execution. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.18.5) cites ‘Father, forgive them’ as proof of Christ's patience and compassion, and Hegesippus, as Eusebius reports (Church History 2.23.16), told how James the brother of Jesus died praying in almost the same words. Origen, in his commentary on Matthew, knew the reading that the sun was eclipsed and suspected that enemies of the faith had introduced it, since an eclipse at full moon was impossible. The unnamed criminals received names in later tradition: Dismas and Gestas in the Acts of Pilate, also called the Gospel of Nicodemus, and Titus and Dumachus in the Arabic Infancy Gospel. Augustine wrestled with the penitent thief's salvation without baptism; he treated his faith and confession as supplying what baptism lacked, and later in his Retractations allowed that he might have been baptized by the water from Christ's side. He also taught that Christ's human soul went down to the dead while his divinity never left paradise, so that the thief could be with him that day.

The punctuation of verse 43 became a question as Christians debated the state of the dead. The eleventh-century Byzantine commentator Theophylact reported that some placed the pause after ‘today’; that reading was taken up by E. W. Bullinger's Companion Bible, the Jehovah's Witnesses' New World Translation, and many Seventh-day Adventist writers. Luke's picture of Pilate and the crowd shaped the church's attitude to Jews for centuries. Jack T. Sanders (The Jews in Luke-Acts, 1987) argued that Luke is deeply hostile to the Jewish people, Jacob Jervell (Luke and the People of God, 1972) that Luke writes for a church that sees itself as restored Israel, and Jeremy Cohen (Christ Killers, 2007) traced how the passion narratives were used to brand Jews as killers of Christ, a charge the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) rejected. Modern scholars have also studied Luke's distinctive details: Martin Dibelius (1915) and Harold Hoehner (1972) on Herod, Dennis Sylva (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1986) on the torn curtain, whose placement just before Jesus' prayer he linked with Jesus' communion with the Father, and Raymond Brown (The Death of the Messiah, 1994) on the whole narrative.

The chapter fills the church's worship. The Revised Common Lectionary reads Luke 22:14-23:56 as the Passion Gospel for Palm Sunday in Year C, and 23:33-43 on the feast of Christ the King in the same year, pairing the crucified King with the kingship of Christ. The Byzantine liturgy's prayer before communion asks to be remembered like the thief, and Holy Friday matins sings of the wise thief. The Taizé community's chant ‘Jesus, remember me’, set by Jacques Berthier (1978), repeats verse 42. The meeting with the women of Jerusalem became a station in the Way of the Cross, and the three sayings became three of the Seven Last Words, set by Joseph Haydn (1787) among many others. Krzysztof Penderecki's St Luke Passion, first performed in Münster Cathedral in 1966, sets Luke's text in Latin with psalms and hymns.
text:
English Bibles differ in several places in this chapter.

Verse 17, ‘For of necessity he must release one unto them at the feast’ (KJV), is absent from the earliest manuscripts, among them P75, Codex Alexandrinus, and Codex Vaticanus, and Codex Bezae places a similar sentence after verse 19. It appears to be a scribal explanation drawn from Mark 15:6 and Matthew 27:15, and modern Bibles print it in a footnote, which is why their numbering skips from 16 to 18.

The prayer in verse 34, ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’, is the chapter's great textual question. It is absent from P75, Vaticanus, the first hand of Bezae, Codex Washingtonianus, the Sinaitic Syriac, and the Sahidic Coptic, and it is present in Sinaiticus, most later manuscripts, Tatian's Diatessaron, and Irenaeus in the second century. The UBS and Nestle-Aland editions print it in double brackets; most English Bibles print it with a note. Those who think it was added point to the strength of the early omitting witnesses and suggest it was drawn from oral tradition, perhaps shaped by Stephen's prayer (Acts 7:60). Those who think it was removed, among them Adolf von Harnack and Nathan Eubank (Journal of Biblical Literature, 2010), point out that early readers took the prayer as forgiveness for the Jews and that after the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 some believed God had plainly not forgiven them, which gave scribes a motive to cut it. The saying is thoroughly Lukan in its themes (6:27-28, 23:28, Acts 3:17), and many who doubt that Luke wrote it here still regard it as a genuine memory of Jesus.

In verse 38 the King James Version adds that the inscription was written in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters, words that the earliest manuscripts, P75 and Vaticanus among them, lack; they probably came from John 19:20. In verse 42 the later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read ‘he said unto Jesus, Lord, remember me’, where the earliest have ‘Jesus, remember me’; P75 and Vaticanus, followed by the Nestle-Aland text, read ‘into your kingdom’, while many other manuscripts, followed by the SBL Greek New Testament, read ‘in your kingdom’, a difference between entering kingly rule at the ascension and returning with it. In verse 45 the earliest manuscripts (P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) read tou hēliou eklipontos, ‘the sun's light failed’, a verb that can mean an eclipse; most later ones read ‘the sun was darkened’, probably a correction. In verse 53 Codex Bezae adds that Joseph placed over the tomb a stone that twenty men could scarcely roll.

teach.big: The innocent King is condemned in the place of the guilty and, from the cross, forgives his enemies, opens paradise to a dying criminal, and entrusts himself to the Father.

outline.t: Jesus is accused of crimes against Caesar that his own teaching refutes, and the governor finds no case against him.
Herod wanted a spectacle, not the truth; Jesus' silence before curiosity and contempt is itself a judgment.
Pilate knows Jesus is innocent and hands him over anyway, and the guilty Barabbas goes free in his place.
Simon carries the cross behind Jesus, and Jesus turns the women's grief toward the judgment coming on those who reject him.
Crucified between criminals, Jesus prays for his executioners and refuses to save himself so that he may save others.
One criminal mocks and one repents; the King answers a dying man's plea with the promise of paradise today.
Darkness and a torn curtain surround the death of the Son who commits his spirit to the Father, and a Gentile soldier declares him righteous.
A righteous council member buries Jesus, and faithful women watch, so that the tomb is known and the Sabbath rest is kept.

teach.pitfalls:
The most damaging misuse of this chapter has been to blame ‘the Jews’ for the death of Jesus. Luke names specific leaders, a crowd at the governor's court, Herod, Pilate, and Roman soldiers; he also shows Jewish women mourning, crowds going home grieving, and a righteous member of the council burying Jesus, and Jesus prays for forgiveness for those who acted in ignorance. Teachers should say so plainly. A second error treats the thief's salvation as permission to postpone repentance. The criminal had no earlier chance that the text mentions, and his confession is costly and honest; the point is grace to the undeserving, not a strategy for delay.

A third error builds a detailed map of the afterlife on verse 43. The verse promises fellowship with Christ ‘today’; it does not answer every question about where paradise is or what the state of the dead is like, and faithful Christians differ on those questions. A fourth hurries past Pilate's weakness as though it were someone else's sin; his choice to do what he knew was wrong under pressure is among the most ordinary sins in the chapter. Finally, avoid preaching verse 34 as though its textual status did not matter; say honestly that some early manuscripts lack it, and that its teaching is found throughout Luke and Acts whatever one concludes.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will press on the dying and on those sitting with them. The promise of verse 43 has been read at countless bedsides, and it should be offered with care, neither turning it into a guarantee about someone whose heart is unknown nor withholding its comfort from those who turn to Christ at the end. It will press on those carrying guilt for a life badly lived, who may identify with the criminal who said ‘we are punished justly’; let them hear the ‘today’ of Jesus' answer. It will press on those who have suffered injustice at the hands of authorities and crowds, and who find ‘Father, forgive them’ hard or impossible to pray; the prayer is Jesus' own before it is a demand on them, and forgiveness in Scripture does not deny that a wrong was done. And those grieving a death that seemed meaningless can watch Luke's faithful women, who stayed, watched, and prepared spices, not knowing yet what the third day would bring.

hard.q: Did Jesus promise the criminal that he would be in paradise that very day, and what does that say about the state of the dead?
hard.a:
The strongest objection comes from those who hold that the dead sleep until the resurrection. Greek manuscripts of Luke's time had little or no punctuation, so the sentence ‘Amen soi legō sēmeron met' emou esē en tō paradeisō’ can be divided before or after ‘today’. Seventh-day Adventist writers, E. W. Bullinger's Companion Bible, and the Jehovah's Witnesses' New World Translation read ‘Truly I tell you today, you will be with me in paradise’: Jesus solemnly promises on the day of his death that the man will share his kingdom at the resurrection. The eleventh-century commentator Theophylact knew of readers who punctuated this way, and some cite the word order of the Curetonian Syriac in support. They point out that Jesus was not in heaven that day, since he told Mary Magdalene after his resurrection that he had not yet ascended to the Father (John 20:17), and that Scripture often speaks of death as sleep (Daniel 12:2, 1 Thessalonians 4:13-16). A Jewish reader might add that in the rabbinic tradition the Garden of Eden could name the destiny of the righteous (b. Berakhot 28b), so the saying need not imply anything about the time between death and resurrection.

Most interpreters, Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant, read ‘today’ with what follows. Jesus uses the formula ‘truly I tell you’ many times in the Gospels, and it never elsewhere includes ‘today’, which would add nothing, since he could hardly be speaking on another day. ‘Today’ is also one of Luke's favorite words for the arrival of salvation (2:11, 4:21, 19:5, 19:9). And the criminal asked to be remembered in the future, when Jesus came into his kingdom; the reply answers with something sooner. Within that majority there are different accounts of paradise. Many early fathers and later Catholic theology held that the righteous dead waited in a region of the realm of the dead, sometimes called Abraham's bosom (16:22), until Christ descended there and opened heaven, and Augustine taught that Christ's soul went to the dead while his divinity remained in paradise. Most Protestants identify paradise with the presence of Christ in heaven, drawing on Paul's language of the third heaven and paradise (2 Corinthians 12:2-4) and of departing to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23). Both readings see the verse as a promise of conscious fellowship with Christ after death and before the resurrection of the body, which the creeds confess as the final hope. Christians still differ on how to describe the intermediate state, and the verse does not settle every question; what it plainly gives is a crucified King's word to a dying man, in the first person: with me.

hard.q: Does Luke shift the blame for Jesus' death from Rome to the Jewish people, and has this chapter been misused?
hard.a:
The objection has been pressed with force by Jewish and Christian scholars alike. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment that only the governor could order, yet Luke has Pilate declare Jesus innocent three times and hand him over ‘to their will’ (verse 25), which can be read as making the crowd and its leaders the real executioners. Paul Winter (On the Trial of Jesus, 1961) argued that the Gospels progressively shift responsibility from Rome to the Jews, and Jack T. Sanders (The Jews in Luke-Acts, 1987) read Luke-Acts as condemning the Jewish people as a whole. The consequences were real. From Melito of Sardis in the second century onward, Christian preaching charged Israel with killing God, and Jeremy Cohen's Christ Killers (2007) traces how that charge fueled contempt and violence for centuries, down to controversies over modern passion plays and films.

The responses begin with the text. Luke names particular actors: the chief priests and rulers, a crowd at the governor's court, Herod and his soldiers, Pilate, and Roman soldiers who crucify and mock. He also shows many Jews who do not share their guilt: the women of Jerusalem who mourn (verse 27), the crowds who go home beating their breasts (verse 48), and Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who had not consented (verses 50-51). In Acts, Peter tells the people of Jerusalem that they acted in ignorance, as did their rulers, and calls them to repentance (Acts 3:17-19), and the same apostles pray that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the peoples of Israel all took part (Acts 4:27). Luke's Pilate is not excused: he knows the truth and yields anyway, and Helen Bond (Pontius Pilate in History and Interpretation, 1998) has argued that Mark's Pilate is a shrewd manager of a crowd rather than a helpless one, and has traced how each evangelist shapes his portrait. Jacob Jervell (Luke and the People of God, 1972) argued that Luke writes as a Jewish-Christian insider for whom the division is within Israel, not between Israel and the church. The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) stated that what happened in the passion cannot be charged against all Jews then living or against Jews today, and Christian theology has long taught that the deepest cause of Jesus' death is the sin of all humanity and his own willing gift of himself. Whether Luke's emphasis on Pilate's reluctance is historical memory or apologetic shaping remains debated among historians; the prayer ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ is the answer the cross itself gives to the question of blame.

observe: How many times does Pilate declare Jesus innocent, and who else in the chapter says he has done nothing wrong?
What does each of the three groups at the cross say to Jesus (verses 35-39), and what do their words have in common?
What do the women from Galilee see and do in verses 49 and 55-56?
interpret: Why do you think Luke includes the scene before Herod, and what does Jesus' silence there communicate?
What is the irony in the taunt ‘He saved others; let Him save Himself’?
What does the conversation between Jesus and the two criminals teach about faith, repentance, and grace?
apply: Pilate knew Jesus was innocent and handed him over anyway. Where are you tempted to do what you know is wrong because of pressure from others?
The criminal brought nothing but an honest confession and a request. What does his story say to someone who thinks it is too late?
Jesus prayed for those who were killing him. Whom would you find it hardest to pray for in that way, and what would it cost you to begin?
